{{Short description|Formulae for viscous and incompressible fluid flow at small Reynolds numbers}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2022}}
In [[fluid dynamics]], the '''Oseen equations''' (or '''Oseen flow''') describe the flow of a [[viscosity|viscous]] and [[Incompressible flow|incompressible]] [[fluid]] at small [[Reynolds number]]s, as formulated by [[Carl Wilhelm Oseen]] in 1910. Oseen flow is an improved description of these flows, as compared to [[Stokes flow]], with the (partial) inclusion of [[Navier–Stokes equations#Convective acceleration|convective acceleration]].<ref name=Batch240>Batchelor (2000), §4.10, pp. 240–246.</ref>

Oseen's work is based on the experiments of [[George Gabriel Stokes|G.G. Stokes]], who had studied the falling of a sphere through a [[viscosity|viscous]] fluid. He developed a correction term, which included [[inertia]]l factors, for the flow velocity used in Stokes' calculations, to solve the problem known as [[Stokes' paradox]]. His approximation leads to an improvement to Stokes' calculations.

==Equations==

The Oseen equations are, in case of an object moving with a steady [[flow velocity]] '''U''' through the fluid—which is at rest far from the object—and in a [[frame of reference]] attached to the object:<ref name=Batch240/>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  -\rho\mathbf{U}\cdot\nabla\mathbf{u} &= -\nabla p\, +\, \mu \nabla^2 \mathbf{u}, \\
  \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u} &= 0,
\end{align}</math>
where
* '''u''' is the disturbance in flow velocity induced by the moving object, ''i.e.'' the total flow velocity in the frame of reference moving with the object is −'''U''' + '''u''',
* ''p'' is the [[pressure]],
* ''ρ'' is the [[density]] of the fluid,
* ''μ'' is the [[dynamic viscosity]],
* &nabla; is the [[gradient]] operator, and
* &nabla;<sup>2</sup> is the [[Laplace operator]].

The boundary conditions for the Oseen flow around a rigid object are:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \mathbf{u} &= \mathbf{U} & & \text{at the object surface}, \\
  \mathbf{u} &\to 0 & & \text{and} \quad p \to p_{\infty} \quad \text{for} \quad r \to \infty,
\end{align}</math>
with ''r'' the distance from the object's center, and ''p''<sub>∞</sub> the undisturbed pressure far from the object.

==Longitudinal and transversal waves==
Source:<ref name="Lagerstrom, Paco Axel 1996">Lagerstrom, Paco Axel. Laminar flow theory. Princeton University Press, 1996.</ref>

A fundamental property of Oseen's equation is that the general solution can be split into ''longitudinal'' and ''transversal'' waves.

A solution <math>\left(\mathbf{u}_\text{L}, p'\right)</math> is a '''longitudinal''' wave if the velocity is irrotational and hence the viscous term drops out. The equations become
<math display="block">
  {\mathbf{u}_\text{L}}_t + U{\mathbf{u}_\text{L}}_x + \frac{1}{\rho}\nabla p = 0, \quad
  \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}_\text{L} = 0, \quad
  \nabla \times \mathbf{u}_\text{L} = 0
</math>

In consequence
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{u}_\text{L} = \nabla\phi, \quad
  \nabla^2\phi = 0, \quad
  p' = p - p_\infty = -\rho U\mathbf{u}_\text{L}
</math>

Velocity is derived from [[potential flow|potential theory]] and pressure is from linearized Bernoulli's equations.

A solution <math>(\mathbf{u}_\text{T}, 0)</math> is a '''transversal''' wave if the pressure <math>p'</math> is identically zero and the velocity field is solenoidal. The equations are
<math display="block">
  {\mathbf{u}_\text{T}}_t + U{\mathbf{u}_\text{T}}_x = \nu\nabla^2\mathbf{u}_\text{T}, \quad
  \nabla\cdot\mathbf{u_T} = 0.
</math>

Then the complete Oseen solution is given by
<math display="block">\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_\text{L} + \mathbf{u}_\text{T}</math>

a [[splitting theorem]] due to [[Horace Lamb]].<ref>Lamb, Horace. Hydrodynamics. Cambridge university press, 1932.</ref> The splitting is unique if conditions at infinity (say <math>\mathbf{u} = 0,\ p = p_\infty</math>) are specified.

For certain Oseen flows, further splitting of transversal wave into irrotational and rotational component is possible <math>\mathbf{u}_\text{T} = \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2.</math> Let <math>\chi</math> be the scalar function which satisfies <math>U\chi_x = \nu\nabla^2\chi</math> and vanishes at infinity and conversely let <math>\mathbf{u}_\text{T} = (u_\text{T}, v_\text{T})</math> be given such that <math display="inline">\int_{-\infty}^\infty v_\text{T} \, dy = 0</math>, then the transversal wave is
<math display="block">
  \mathbf{u}_\text{T} = -\frac{\nu}{U}\nabla\chi + \chi\mathbf{i}, \quad
  \mathbf{u}_\text{1} = -\frac{\nu}{U}\nabla\chi, \quad
  \mathbf{u}_\text{2} = \chi \mathbf{i}.
</math>
where <math>\chi</math> is determined from <math display="inline">\chi = \frac{U}{\nu} \int_y^\infty v_T \, dy</math> and <math>\mathbf{i}</math> is the [[unit vector]]. Neither <math>\mathbf{u}_1</math> or <math>\mathbf{u}_2</math> are transversal by itself, but <math>\mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2</math> is transversal. Therefore,
<math display="block">\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}_\text{L} + \mathbf{u}_\text{T} = \mathbf{u}_\text{L} + \mathbf{u}_1 + \mathbf{u}_2</math>

The only rotational component is being <math>\mathbf{u}_2</math>.

==Fundamental solutions==
Source:<ref name="Lagerstrom, Paco Axel 1996"/>

The [[fundamental solution]] due to a singular point force embedded in an Oseen flow is the '''Oseenlet'''.  The closed-form [[fundamental solution]]s for the generalized unsteady Stokes and Oseen flows associated with arbitrary time-dependent translational and rotational motions have been derived for the Newtonian<ref>{{cite journal | title = Generalized fundamental solutions for unsteady viscous flows | journal = Physical Review E | date = 2001 | first = Jian-Jun | last = Shu |author2=Chwang, A.T. | volume = 63 | issue = 5 | article-number = 051201 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevE.63.051201 | pmid = 11414893 |arxiv = 1403.3247 |bibcode = 2001PhRvE..63e1201S | s2cid = 22258027 }}</ref> and micropolar<ref>{{cite journal | title = Fundamental solutions for micropolar fluids | journal = Journal of Engineering Mathematics | date = 2008 | first = Jian-Jun | last = Shu |author2=Lee, J.S. | volume = 61 | issue = 1 | pages = 69–79 | doi = 10.1007/s10665-007-9160-8 |arxiv = 1402.5023 | bibcode = 2008JEnMa..61...69S | s2cid = 3450011 }}</ref> fluids.

Using the Oseen equation, [[Horace Lamb]] was able to derive improved expressions for the viscous flow around a sphere in 1911, improving on [[Stokes' law|Stokes law]] towards somewhat higher Reynolds numbers.<ref name=Batch240/> Also, Lamb derived—for the first time—a solution for the viscous flow around a circular cylinder.<ref name=Batch240/>

The solution to the response of a singular force <math>\mathbf{f}</math> when no external boundaries are present be written as
<math display="block">U \mathbf{u}_x + \frac{1}{\rho}\nabla p -\nu\nabla^2\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{f}, \quad \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0</math>

If <math>\mathbf{f}=\delta(q,q_o)\mathbf{a}</math>, where <math>\delta(q,q_o)</math> is the singular force concentrated at the point <math>q_o</math> and <math>q</math> is an arbitrary point and <math>\mathbf{a}</math> is the given vector, which gives the direction of the singular force, then in the absence of boundaries, the velocity and pressure is derived from the fundamental tensor <math>\Gamma(q,q_o)</math> and the fundamental vector <math>\Pi(q,q_o)</math>
<math display="block">\mathbf{u}(q) = \Gamma(q,q_o) \mathbf{a}, \quad p'=p-p_\infty = \Pi(q,q_o)\cdot\mathbf{a}</math>

Now if <math>\mathbf{f}</math> is arbitrary function of space, the solution for an unbounded domain is
<math display="block">\mathbf{u}(q) = \int \Gamma(q,q_o) \mathbf{f} (q_o) dq_o, \quad p'(q) =  \int \Pi(q,q_o) \cdot\mathbf{f} (q_o) dq_o</math>
where <math>dq_o</math> is the [[infinitesimal]] volume/area element around the point <math>q_o</math>.

===Two-dimensional===
[[Without loss of generality]] <math>q_o=(0,0)</math> taken at the origin and <math>q=(x,y)</math>. Then the fundamental tensor and vector are
<math display="block">
  \Gamma = \begin{pmatrix}
    \frac{\partial A}{\partial x} &  \frac{\partial A}{\partial y} \\
    \frac{\partial A}{\partial y} & -\frac{\partial A}{\partial x} 
  \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{2\pi\nu} e^{\lambda x} K_o(\lambda r)  
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & 0  \\
    0 & 1 
  \end{pmatrix},\quad
  \Pi = \frac{\rho}{2\pi} \nabla (\ln r)
</math>
where
<math display="block">
  \lambda = \frac{U}{2\nu},\quad
  r^2 = x^2 + y^2,\quad
  A = -\frac{1}{2\pi U}\left[\ln r + e^{\lambda x} K_o(\lambda r)\right]
</math>
where <math>K_o(\lambda r)</math> is the [[modified Bessel function of the second kind]] of order zero.

===Three-dimensional===
Without loss of generality <math>q_o = (0, 0, 0)</math> taken at the origin and <math>q = (x, y, z)</math>. Then the fundamental tensor and vector are
<math display="block">
  \Gamma = \begin{pmatrix}
    \frac{\partial A}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial B}{\partial x} & \frac{\partial C}{\partial x} \\
    \frac{\partial A}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial B}{\partial y} & \frac{\partial C}{\partial y} \\
    \frac{\partial A}{\partial z} & \frac{\partial B}{\partial z} & \frac{\partial C}{\partial z} 
  \end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{4\pi\nu} \frac{e^{-\lambda(r - x)}}{r}  
  \begin{pmatrix}
    1 & 0 & 0 \\
    0 & 1 & 0 \\
    0 & 0 & 1 
  \end{pmatrix},\quad
  \Pi = -\frac{\rho}{4\pi} \nabla \left(\frac{1}{r}\right)
</math>
where
{{unbulleted list | style = padding-left: 1.5em
| <math>\lambda = \frac{U}{2\nu}, </math>
| <math>r^2 = x^2 + y^2 + z^2, </math>
| <math>A =  \frac{1}{4\pi U} \frac{1 - e^{-\lambda (r - x)}}{r}, </math>
| <math>B = -\frac{1}{4\pi U} \frac{\left[1 - e^{-\lambda (r - x)}\right]y}{r(r - x)}, </math>
| <math>C = -\frac{1}{4\pi U} \frac{\left[1 - e^{-\lambda (r - x)}\right]z}{r(r - x)} </math>
}}

==Calculations==
Oseen considered the sphere to be stationary and the fluid to be flowing with a [[flow velocity]] (<math>U</math>) at an infinite distance from the sphere. Inertial terms were neglected in Stokes' calculations.<ref name=Fung/> It is a limiting solution when the Reynolds number tends to zero. When the Reynolds number is small and finite, such as 0.1, correction for the inertial term is needed. Oseen substituted the following flow velocity values into the [[Navier-Stokes equations]].
<math display="block">u_1 = u + u_1', \qquad u_2 = u_2', \qquad u_3 = u_3'.</math>

Inserting these into the Navier-Stokes equations and neglecting the quadratic terms in the primed quantities leads to the derivation of Oseen's approximation:
<math display="block">u{\partial u_1' \over \partial x_1} = -{1 \over \rho}{\partial p \over \partial x_1} + \nu\nabla^2 u_i' \qquad \left({i = 1, 2, 3}\right).</math>

Since the motion is symmetric with respect to <math>x</math> axis and the divergence of the vorticity vector is always zero we get:
<math display="block">\left(\nabla^2 - {U \over 2v}{\partial \over \partial x}\right) \chi = G(x) = 0</math>
the function <math>G(x)</math> can be eliminated by adding to a suitable function in <math>x</math>, is the vorticity function, and the previous function can be written as:
<math display="block">{U \over v}{\partial u' \over \partial x} = \nabla^2 u'</math>
and by some integration the solution for <math>\chi</math> is:
<math display="block">e^{-Ux \over 2v} \chi = {{Ce^{-U\operatorname{Re} \over 2v}} \over \operatorname{Re}} </math>
thus by letting <math>x</math> be the "privileged direction" it produces:
<math display="block">\varphi = {A_0 \over \operatorname{Re}} + A_1{\partial \over \partial x}{1 \over \operatorname{Re}} + A_2{\partial^2 \over \partial x^2}{1 \over \operatorname{Re}} + \ldots</math>

then by applying the three boundary conditions we obtain
<math display="block">C = -{3 \over 2}Ua,\ A_0 = -{3 \over 2}va,\ A_1 = {1 \over 4}Ua^3\ \text{, etc.}</math>
the new improved [[drag coefficient]] now become:
<math display="block">C_\text{d} = {12 \over \operatorname{Re}} \left(1 + {3 \over 8} \operatorname{Re}\right)</math>
and finally, when Stokes' solution was solved on the basis of Oseen's approximation, it showed that the resultant [[drag (force)|drag force]] is given by
<math display="block">F = 6\pi\, \mu\, au\left(1 + {3 \over 8} \operatorname{Re}\right),</math>

where:
* <math>\mathrm{Re} = \rho ua/\mu</math> is the [[Reynolds number]] based on the radius of the sphere, <math>a</math>
* <math>F</math> is the hydrodynamic force
* <math>u</math> is the flow velocity
* <math>\mu\,</math> is the fluid viscosity

The force from Oseen's equation differs from that of Stokes by a factor of
<math display="block">1 + {3 \over 8} \mathrm{Re}.</math>

==Correction to Stokes' solution==

The equations for the perturbation read:<ref>{{harvnb|Mei|2011}}</ref>
<math display="block">\begin{align}
   \nabla u' &~= 0 \\
  u\cdot\nabla u' &~= -\nabla p + \nu\nabla^2 u',
\end{align}</math>
but when the velocity field is:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  u_y &=  u\cos\theta\left({1 + {a^3 \over 2r^3} - {3a \over 2r}}\right) \\
  u_z &= -u\sin\theta\left({1 - {a^3 \over 4r^3} - {3a \over 4r}}\right).
\end{align}</math>

In the far field <math>{r \over a}</math> ≫ 1, the viscous stress is dominated by the last term. That is:
<math display="block">\nabla^2 u' = O\left({a^3 \over r^3}\right).</math>

The inertia term is dominated by the term:
<math display="block">u{\partial u' \over \partial z_1} \sim O\left({a^2 \over r^2}\right).</math>

The error is then given by the ratio:
<math display="block">u {{\partial u' \over \partial z_1} \over {\nu\nabla^2 u'}} = O\left({r \over a}\right).</math>

This becomes unbounded for <math>{r \over a}</math> ≫ 1, therefore the inertia cannot be ignored in the far field. By taking the curl, Stokes equation gives <math>\nabla^2\zeta\, = 0.</math>  Since the body is a source of [[vorticity]], <math>\zeta\,</math> would become unbounded [[logarithm]]ically for large <math>{r \over a}.</math> This is certainly unphysical and is known as [[Stokes' paradox]].

== Solution for a moving sphere in incompressible fluid ==
Consider the case of a solid sphere moving in a stationary liquid with a constant velocity.
The liquid is modeled as an [[incompressible fluid]] (i.e. with constant [[density]]), and being stationary means that its velocity tends towards zero as the distance from the sphere approaches infinity.

For a real body there will be a transient effect due to its acceleration as it begins its motion; however after enough time it will tend towards zero, so that the fluid velocity everywhere will approach the one obtained in the hypothetical case in which the body is already moving for infinite time.

Thus we assume a sphere of radius ''a'' moving at a constant velocity <math>\vec{U}</math>, in an incompressible fluid that is at rest at infinity. We will work in coordinates <math>\vec{x}_m</math> that move along with the sphere with the coordinate center located at the sphere's center. We have:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \vec{u}\left(\left\|{\vec{x}_m}\right\| = a\right) &= \vec{U} \\
  \vec{u}\left(\left\|{\vec{x}_m}\right\| \rightarrow \infty\right) &\rightarrow 0
\end{align}</math>

Since these boundary conditions, as well as the equation of motions, are time invariant (i.e. they are unchanged by shifting the time <math>t \rightarrow t + \Delta t</math>) when expressed in the <math>\vec{x}_m</math> coordinates, the solution depends upon the time only through these coordinates.

The equations of motion are the [[Navier-Stokes equations]] defined in the resting frame coordinates <math>\vec{x} = \vec{x}_m - \vec{U}\cdot t</math>. While spatial derivatives are equal in both coordinate systems, the [[time derivative]] that appears in the equations satisfies:
<math display="block">
   \frac{\partial\vec{u}\left(\vec{x}, t\right)}{\partial t} =
   \sum_i{\frac{d{x_m}_i}{dt} \frac{\partial\vec{u}\left(\vec{x}_m\right)}{\partial{x_m}_i}} =
  -\left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}_m\right)\vec{u}
</math>
where the derivative <math>\vec{\nabla}_m</math> is with respect to the moving coordinates <math>\vec{x}_m</math>. We henceforth omit the ''m'' subscript.

Oseen's approximation sums up to neglecting the term non-linear in <math>\vec{u}</math>. Thus the [[Navier–Stokes equations#Incompressible flow|incompressible Navier-Stokes equations]] become:
<math display="block">\left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\vec{u} + \nu\nabla^2\vec{u} = \frac{1}{\rho}\vec{\nabla}p</math>
for a fluid having [[density]] &rho; and [[Viscosity#Kinematic viscosity|kinematic viscosity]] &nu; = &mu;/&rho; (&mu; being the [[Viscosity#Dynamic (shear) viscosity|dynamic viscosity]]). ''p'' is the [[pressure]].

Due to the [[Continuity equation#Fluid dynamics|continuity equation]] for incompressible fluid <math>\vec{\nabla} \cdot \vec{u} = 0</math>, the solution can be expressed using a [[vector potential]] <math>\vec{\psi}</math>. This turns out to be directed at the <math>\vec{\varphi}</math> direction and its magnitude is equivalent to the [[stream function]] used in two-dimensional problems. It turns out to be:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
     \psi &= Ua^2 \left(-\frac{a}{4r^2}\sin\theta + 3\frac{1 - \cos\theta}{r\sin\theta}\frac{1 - e^{-\frac{Rr}{4a}(1 + \cos\theta)}}{R}\right) \\
  \vec{u} &= \vec{\nabla}\times(\psi\hat{\varphi}) = \frac{1}{r\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\psi \sin\theta\right)\hat{r} - \frac{1}{r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r\psi\right)\hat{\theta}
\end{align}</math>
where <math>R = 2aU/\nu</math> is [[Reynolds number]] for the flow close to the sphere.

Note that in some notations <math>\psi</math> is replaced by <math>\Psi = \psi \cdot r\sin\theta</math> so that the derivation of <math>\vec{u}</math> from <math>\Psi</math> is more similar to its derivation from the [[stream function]] in the two-dimensional case (in polar coordinates).

=== Elaboration ===
<math>\psi</math> can be expressed as follows:
<math display="block">\psi = \psi_1 + \psi_2 - \psi_2 e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}</math>

where:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \psi_1 &\equiv -\frac{Ua^3}{4r^2} \sin\theta \\
  \psi_2 &\equiv  \frac{3Ua^2}{Rr} \frac{1 - \cos\theta}{\sin\theta}
\end{align}</math>
<math display="block">k \equiv \frac{R}{4a}</math>, so that <math>\frac{U}{2k} = \frac{2Ua}{R} = \nu</math>.

The [[vector Laplacian]] of a vector of the type <math>V(r, \theta)\hat{\varphi}</math> [[Del in cylindrical and spherical coordinates#Del formulae|reads]]:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  &\nabla^2\left(V(r, \theta)\hat{\varphi}\right) =
    \hat{\varphi} \cdot \left(\nabla^2 - \frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\right)V(r, \theta) =\\
  &\hat{\varphi} \cdot \left[
    \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}V(r, \theta)\right) +
    \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}V(r, \theta)\right) -
    \frac{V(r, \theta)}{r^2\sin^2\theta}
  \right]
\end{align}</math>.

It can thus be calculated that:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \nabla^2\left(\psi_1\hat{\varphi}\right) &= 0 \\
  \nabla^2\left(\psi_2\hat{\varphi}\right) &= 0
\end{align}</math>

Therefore:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \nabla^2\vec{\psi}
    &= -\nabla^2\left(\psi_2 e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi}\right) \\
    &= -\left(\psi_2\nabla^2 e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)} + 2\frac{\partial\psi_2}{\partial r}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)} +
        \frac{2}{r^2}\frac{\partial\psi_2}{\partial\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\right)\hat{\varphi} \\
    &= -\frac{6Ua^2}{R}\sin\theta\left(\frac{k^2}{r} + \frac{k}{r^2}\right)e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi}
\end{align}</math>

Thus the [[vorticity]] is:
<math display="block">
  \vec{\omega} \equiv \vec{\nabla}\times\vec{u} = -\nabla^2\vec{\psi} =
  \frac{6Ua^2}{R}\sin\theta\left(\frac{k^2}{r} + \frac{k}{r^2}\right)e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi}
</math>

where we have used the [[divergenceless|vanishing of the divergence]] of <math>\vec{\psi}</math> to relate the [[vector laplacian#Definition|vector laplacian]] and a double [[Curl (mathematics)|curl]].

The equation of motion's left hand side is the curl of the following:
<math display="block">
  \left(\vec{U}\cdot\vec{\nabla}\right)\vec{\psi} + \nu\nabla^2\vec{\psi} =
  \left(\vec{U}\cdot\vec{\nabla}\right)\vec{\psi} - \nu\vec{\omega}
</math>

We calculate the derivative separately for each term in <math>\psi</math>.

Note that:
<math display="block">\vec{U} = U\left(\cos\theta\hat{r} - \sin\theta\hat{\theta}\right)</math>

And also:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
                \frac{\partial\psi_2}{\partial r} &= -\frac{1}{r}\psi_2 \\
  \sin\theta\frac{\partial\psi_2}{\partial\theta} &= \psi_2
\end{align}</math>

We thus have:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\left(\psi_1\hat{\varphi}\right)
    &= U\left(\cos\theta\frac{\partial \psi_1}{\partial r} - \frac{1}{r}\sin\theta\frac{\partial\psi_1}{\partial\theta}\right)\hat{\varphi}
     = \frac{3U^2 a^3}{4r^3}\sin\theta\cos\theta\hat{\varphi} \\
  \left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\left(\psi_2\hat{\varphi}\right)
    &= U\left(\cos\theta\frac{\partial \psi_2}{\partial r} - \frac{1}{r}\sin\theta\frac{\partial\psi_2}{\partial\theta}\right)\hat{\varphi}
     = -U\frac{1}{r}(1 + \cos\theta)\psi_2\hat{\varphi}
     = -\frac{3U^2 a^2}{Rr^2}\sin\theta\hat{\varphi} \\
  \left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\left(-\psi_2 e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi}\right)
    &= -e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\left(\left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\left(\psi_2\hat{\varphi}) + \psi_2\left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\left(-kr(1 + \cos\theta\right)\hat{\varphi}\right)\right) \\
    &= U\psi_2 e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\left(\frac{1}{r}(1 + \cos\theta) + \cos\theta\frac{\partial(kr(1 + \cos\theta))}{\partial r} - \frac{1}{r}\sin\theta\frac{\partial(kr(1 + \cos\theta))}{\partial\theta}\right)\hat{\varphi} \\
    &= U\psi_2(1 + \cos\theta)\left(\frac{1}{r} + k\right)e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi}
     = \frac{3U^2 a^2}{R}\sin\theta\left(\frac{1}{r^2} + \frac{k}{r}\right)e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\hat{\varphi} \\
    &= \frac{U}{2k}\vec{\omega} = \nu\vec{\omega}
\end{align}</math>

Combining all the terms we have:
<math display="block">
  \left(\vec{U} \cdot \vec{\nabla}\right)\vec{\psi} + \nu\nabla^2\vec{\psi} =
  \left(\frac{3U^2 a^3}{4r^3}\sin\theta\cos\theta - \frac{3U^2 a^2}{Rr^2}\sin\theta\right)\hat{\varphi}
</math>

Taking the curl, we find an expression that is equal to <math>1/\rho</math> times the gradient of the following function, which is the pressure:
<math display="block">p = p_0 - \frac{3\mu Ua}{2r^2}\cos\theta + \frac{\rho U^2 a^3}{4r^3}\left(3\cos^2\theta - 1\right)</math>

where <math>p_0</math> is the pressure at infinity, <math>\theta</math>.is the polar angle originated from the opposite side of the front [[stagnation point]] (<math>\theta = \pi</math> where is the front stagnation point).

Also, the velocity is derived by taking the curl of <math>\vec{\psi}</math>:
<math display="block">
  \vec{u} = U\left[
      -\frac{a^3}{2r^3}\cos\theta + \frac{3a^2}{Rr^2}
      - \frac{3a^2}{R}\left(\frac{1}{r^2} + \frac{k}{r}[1 - \cos\theta]\right)e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}
    \right]\hat{r}
  - U\left[\frac{a^3}{4r^3}\sin\theta + \frac{3a^2}{Rr}k\sin\theta e^{-kr(1 + \cos\theta)}\right]\hat{\theta}
</math>

These ''p'' and ''u'' satisfy the equation of motion and thus constitute the solution to Oseen's approximation.

==Modifications to Oseen's approximation==
One may question, however, whether the correction term was chosen by chance, because in a frame of reference moving with the sphere, the fluid near the sphere is almost at rest, and in that region inertial force is negligible and Stokes' equation is well justified.<ref name=Fung/> Far away from the sphere, the flow velocity approaches ''u'' and Oseen's approximation is more accurate.<ref name=Fung/> But Oseen's equation was obtained applying the equation for the entire flow field. This question was answered by Proudman and Pearson in 1957,<ref>{{harvtxt|Proudman|Pearson|1957}}</ref> who solved the Navier-Stokes equations and gave an improved Stokes' solution in the neighborhood of the sphere and an improved Oseen's solution at infinity, and matched the two solutions in a supposed common region of their validity. They obtained:

<math display="block">F = 6\pi\,\mu\,a U\left(1 + {3 \over 8} \operatorname{Re} + {9 \over 40} \operatorname{Re}^2 \ln \operatorname{Re} + \mathcal{O}\left(\operatorname{Re}^2\right)\right).</math>

==Applications==
The method and formulation for analysis of flow at a very low [[Reynolds number]] is important. The slow motion of small particles in a fluid is common in [[bio-engineering]]. Oseen's drag formulation can be used in connection with flow of fluids under various special conditions, such as: containing particles, sedimentation of particles, [[centrifugation]] or ultracentrifugation of suspensions, colloids, and blood through isolation of tumors and antigens.<ref name="Fung">{{harvtxt|Fung|1997}}</ref> The fluid does not even have to be a liquid, and the particles do not need to be solid. It can be used in a number of applications, such as smog formation and [[atomizer nozzle|atomization]] of liquids.

Blood flow in small vessels, such as [[capillary|capillaries]], is characterized by small [[Reynolds number|Reynolds]] and [[Womersley number]]s. A vessel of diameter of {{nowrap|10 µm}} with a flow of {{nowrap|1 millimetre/second}}, viscosity of {{nowrap|0.02 poise}} for blood, [[density]] of {{nowrap|1 g/cm<sup>3</sup>}} and a heart rate of {{nowrap|2 Hz}}, will have a Reynolds number of 0.005 and a Womersley number of 0.0126. At these small Reynolds and Womersley numbers, the viscous effects of the fluid become predominant. Understanding the movement of these particles is essential for drug delivery and studying [[metastasis]] movements of cancers.
